newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS-NEW ERA DAWNS AS HINGIS NEARS FRENCH FINAL.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-NEW ERA DAWNS AS HINGIS NEARS FRENCH FINAL.

text.p: A new era in women's tennis may have dawned at the French Open with cheerful Martina Hingis taking over from troubled Steffi Graf as the new Paris queen.

Swiss teenager Hingis still has two hurdles to clear but the kind of form she displayed to crush Spain's Arantxa Sanchez Vicario and advance to the last four makes her the clear favourite to succeed five-times champion Graf.
The once almost unbeatable German, who was ousted from the top spot by Hingis last March, saw her bete noire, South African Amanda Coetzer, slam the door on her on Tuesday.
For the first time in more than a decade, she will not be in the semifinals in the French capital.
Graf, who blamed her shock defeat on a lack of confidence, will drop one place to third in the next women's rankings, her lowest position since March, 1987.
Hingis could meanwhile underline her dominance by winning her second grand slam title of the year after the Australian Open.

Only six weeks after undergoing minor knee surgery following a riding accident, the world number one showed she was back at her brilliant best on Tuesday by outclassing Sanchez Vicario, twice a winner here and a finalist the last two years.
"I feel as good as ever," warned Hingis after an impressive display of elegant tennis. "I'm back and I'll be hard to beat."

Hingis, playing her first tournament since she fell off her horse, said she had turned down an offer by Olympic show jumping champion Pierre Durand of France, who had invited her for a ride this week.

"I've got other things to worry about," said the cheerful 16-year-old, wearing her trademark, permanent smile. "I had said before coming here that the real test would be in the first week. I'm playing better and better. I feel confident."

Hingis, who survived a scare in the second round, struggling for over two hours before moving past little-known Italian Gloria Pizzichini, now faces American Monica Seles on Thursday for a place in Saturday's final.

Former teenage wonder Seles, seeded third this year, has attracted little attention since the start of the tournament but nevertheless stayed on course for a fourth triumph after winning on the Paris clay three times in a row from 1990 to 1992.
"I'm not happy with the way I played, I was lucky to win," said Yugoslav-born Seles after needing three sets to beat American Mary Joe Fernandez on Tuesday.

If Hingis has won her three previous encounters with Seles and looks a safe bet, the other semifinal, between ninth seed Iva Majoli of Croatia and Coetzer, the 11th seed, promises to be a hard-fought affair.
Coetzer boosted her confidence by knocking out Graf in straight sets on Tuesday, recording her third win over the German this season.
Majoli earned her first appearance in a grand slam semifinal after winning a gruelling, three-set battle against her doubles partner, unseeded Romanian Ruxandra Dragomir.
The Croat seems to have more weapons in her arsenal than pocket-sized Coetzer, who is brave and consistent from the baseline but lacks power.
Asked if she thought Coetzer could win the tournament, Graf said: "Probably not".
Nobody asked her if she thought Hingis could win. Everybody knew the answer.
Semifinal line-up: 1-Martina Hingis (Switzerland) v 3-Monica Seles (U.S.) 9-Iva Majoli (Croatia) v 11-Amanda Coetzer (South Africa)
